problem: Rounding the segment size up to (n + 3) // 4 makes the first three streams exceed pack()'s MAX_TABLE_LENGTH sooner, so inputs of 262141-262143 bytes that encode on main now raise ValueError (largest encodable input drops from 262143 to 262140 bytes).

The new split changes encode()'s output bytes for every input length not divisible by 4 and can yield an empty 4th stream or a shorter 3rd stream (n=5 gives 2/2/1/0 instead of 1/1/1/2), silently breaking anything that depends on stable output or the old stream layout.
The guard hard-codes 4 instead of MIN_SPLIT_SIZE, unlike every other check in the module, so the constant no longer controls the check.

The ValueError message regressed from 'split needs at least %d bytes, got %d' to 'too short', dropping the function name, the minimum and the actual length that every other error in the file includes.
The change to how split() divides data and to the accepted input size ships with no tests (the repo has none); a boundary test at n=262140/262141 would have caught SEC-1.
Pre-existing: bytes(data) turns an int argument into a zero-filled buffer, so split(5), encode(8) and decode(10) succeed silently instead of raising; the same pattern is at lines 16, 23 and 36.
MIN_SPLIT_SIZE is now dead code because the guard no longer references it.
encode() does not check the input size up front, so an oversized input fails inside pack() with an internal stream-length message instead of naming the input length and the real limit.
Pre-existing: unpack() only rejects lengths that overflow the block, so a corrupted table that under-reports lengths decodes into scrambled output without error.
